candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize acute neurologic complications and time-sensitive interventions for clients experiencing stroke.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — late-window EVT selection in acute ischemic stroke
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize that late-window EVT is a time-sensitive treatment for selected acute ischemic stroke patients with large-vessel occlusion; contemporary selection integrates clinical status and vascular/brain imaging rather than applying a universal 24-hour rule or requiring one historic perfusion-mismatch profile in every case.

options.A: EVT can benefit selected patients presenting 6–24 hours after onset; eligibility uses vascular and brain imaging plus clinical factors, and treatment should proceed as rapidly as possible rather than assuming every late-window patient is eligible.
options.B: All patients with any ischemic stroke are eligible for EVT through 24 hours without regard to vessel occlusion, infarct burden, disability, or imaging findings.
options.C: Late-window EVT is available only when CT or MR perfusion demonstrates the exact DAWN or DEFUSE-3 mismatch profile; other imaging-selection strategies are no longer acceptable.
options.D: Because a 24-hour window exists for selected patients, time to reperfusion no longer affects outcome once the patient is within that window.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline recommends EVT for selected large-vessel-occlusion patients in the 6–24-hour window using clinical and imaging criteria. DAWN and DEFUSE-3 established benefit using advanced tissue-selection approaches, but subsequent large-core trials expanded the evidence base and the 2026 guideline no longer makes one specific perfusion-mismatch paradigm the universal explanation for late-window eligibility. Imaging must identify the occlusion and assess ischemic burden, and faster treatment remains important because reperfusion benefit is time dependent. B ignores selection criteria. C is too restrictive under current evidence. D falsely treats the late window as time-insensitive.
candidate.source_claim_supported: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline supports EVT through 24 hours for selected LVO patients using clinical and imaging criteria, while preserving the time-sensitive nature of reperfusion and allowing a broader evidence-based imaging approach than a universal DAWN/DEFUSE-3 mismatch requirement.
candidate.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidate.source_locator: Section 4.7.2 Endovascular Thrombectomy for Adults: recommendations for selected anterior-circulation proximal LVO patients presenting 6–24 hours after symptom onset based on clinical and imaging characteristics. Section 3.2 Initial, Vascular, and Multimodal Imaging Approaches and recommendation-support text: imaging identifies LVO and ischemic tissue burden; advanced tissue imaging was used in DAWN/DEFUSE-3 and many later trials, but multiple imaging approaches now inform selection. Supportive text emphasizes that EVT benefit is time dependent and evaluation/treatment should be performed as rapidly as possible.
candidate.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidate.stem: A client with acute ischemic stroke from a large-vessel occlusion presents in a late treatment window. Which statement best reflects the 2026 AHA/ASA approach to endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) selection?
